blocks.text: **The problem.** Given an integer `n`, return `true` if it's a power of two — `n == 2ˣ` for some integer `x ≥ 0` — and `false` otherwise.

blocks.alt: 16 halves to 8, 4, 2 and finally 1, the base case, so 16 is a power of two. 12 halves to 6 and then 3, which is odd and not 1, so 12 is not a power of two.

elements.text: a power of two halves cleanly all the way down to 1
elements.originalText: a power of two halves cleanly all the way down to 1

blocks.code:
n = 1    ->  true    (2^0)
n = 16   ->  true    (2^4)
n = 12   ->  false
n = 0    ->  false
n = -8   ->  false

blocks.text: The idea: halve until you can't

If `n` is a power of two bigger than 1, it's even and `n / 2` is also a power of two. So: 1 is a power of two (the base case); anything below 1 or any odd number other than 1 isn't; and an even number is a power of two exactly when its half is. Each call halves `n`, so there are only about log₂ n calls.

blocks.caption: Each call halves n, until it reaches 1 or an odd number.

blocks.text: **Time O(log n), space O(log n)** for the call stack — at most 31 calls for a 32-bit int.
2. The same idea as a loop

In binary, a power of two is a single 1 followed by zeros: 16 is `10000`. Subtracting 1 flips that 1 and every zero after it: 15 is `01111`. So `n & (n − 1)` is zero exactly for powers of two (and for 0, which the `n > 0` check rules out).

blocks.code:
def is_power_of_two(n):
    return n > 0 and (n & (n - 1)) == 0  # exactly one 1-bit

blocks.text: **Time O(1), space O(1).** The recursive version is the one to reason with; the bit trick is the one interviewers hope you know.

blocks.alt: Recursion: O(log n) time, O(log n) space. Loop: O(log n) time, O(1) space. n & (n - 1): O(1) time, O(1) space.

items: **n = 0 and negative numbers** — false; the bit trick needs the `n > 0` check.
**The largest power of two in an int** — 2³⁰ = 1073741824: true; 2³¹ − 1: false.
**-2147483648** — its bit pattern is a single 1, so the `n > 0` check is what makes it false.
**Power of Three** — the same halving recursion with `% 3` and `/ 3`.
**Power of Four** — a power of two whose single 1-bit sits in an even position.
**Number of 1 Bits** — `n & (n − 1)` clears the lowest 1-bit; count how many times until n is 0.
